prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Terrible, God, Mechanical

outputs.L1: Gravity accounts for the distance between weight and mass. It can also mean alarming importance. Human bones are so full of gravity it is hard for us to swim. I lost my glasses chasing a branch in the ocean, which is far too deep to dredge. Sometimes I imagine the sea is made of actual tears; this would explain the salt. Think of all the disconsolate toddlers weeping right now into the earth. The tears must go somewhere. It is important to consider everything, to name what we are able. Oceans give us rain, but we do not call rain ocean. Knot a dozen rats together by the tail and you have a roi de rats, which is harder than rain to hear in the night and far less welcome. Who mourns a rat king—frustrated, chthonic, always the biter, never the bitten? They give us the evil we need to stay moored to good. Still, I would break any promise to avoid finding one. O Terrible God of the Mechanical Age, I am your favorite pilgrim, yet even I am finding it impossible to speak to you now without asking for protection.
outputs.L2:
Gravity explains the separation between mass and weight; it can also signify a frightening kind of seriousness. Human bones carry so much heaviness that swimming is difficult for us. I once lost my glasses while pursuing a branch in the ocean, a place much too deep to be searched by dredging. At times I picture the sea as being made of real tears, which would account for its salt. Consider every inconsolable toddler crying into the world at this very moment: those tears have to end up somewhere. We must try to take everything into account, to give names to whatever we can. Oceans provide the rain, yet we do not call rain an ocean.

Tie twelve rats together by their tails and you have a rat king, a roi de rats—something more difficult to bear hearing at night than rain, and much less desired. Who grieves for a rat king: thwarted, underworldly, always the creature that bites and never the one bitten? They supply the darkness we require in order to remain anchored to goodness. Even so, I would betray any vow if it meant I could avoid discovering one.

O dreadful God of the Machine Age, I am your most beloved pilgrim, and still, even for me, it has become nearly impossible to address you now without begging to be kept safe.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents gravity not only as a physical force, but also as a symbol of emotional and existential heaviness. On one level, gravity is the natural power that pulls bodies toward the earth, shaping the movements of people, objects, and the world itself. On another level, it suggests the burdens that weigh on the speaker’s mind: grief, fear, memory, and the pressure of trying to make sense of existence. Gravity becomes a way of describing both literal weight and the invisible weight of human experience.

The speaker also reflects on the ocean as something vast, distant, and almost unreachable. It is not simply a body of water, but a place connected to loss and longing. Images of tears, salt, and rain link the ocean to human sorrow, suggesting that personal grief is part of something much larger and more ancient. The ocean becomes a symbol of what cannot be fully grasped or recovered. It holds absence, memory, and emotional depth, remaining both familiar and impossible to possess.

Throughout the poem, there is an emphasis on the human need to name things and to understand the relationships between them. The speaker seems aware that the connections they make may be strange, incomplete, or uncertain, yet the act of naming still matters. To name something is to try to bring it closer, to give it shape, and to make it less overwhelming. Even when meaning is unstable, the poem suggests that humans continue searching for patterns because understanding is a form of survival.

The image of the rat king introduces something disturbing and ominous. Traditionally, a rat king is a grotesque cluster of rats tangled together by their tails, and in the poem it represents what is frightening, unwelcome, and associated with darkness or evil. This image may suggest corruption, entrapment, or the presence of something monstrous beneath the surface of ordinary life. It contrasts sharply with the speaker’s desire for clarity and protection, embodying a force that feels chaotic and threatening.

Finally, the speaker addresses a terrible modern god, suggesting a world in which old forms of faith may feel broken or inadequate. This god is not comforting or benevolent, but frightening, perhaps connected to the violence, uncertainty, or machinery of modern life. Even so, the speaker admits a need for protection. There is a tension between fear and dependence, disbelief and prayer. The speaker struggles to pray, yet the need for shelter, mercy, or guidance remains. This conflict gives the poem much of its emotional force: it portrays a person trying to survive in a world that feels heavy, mysterious, and spiritually unstable.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a surreal and poetic meditation on gravity, loss, oceans, naming, fear, and faith. Rather than treating these subjects separately, it connects them through a series of strange and vivid images in which the physical world becomes a reflection of emotional and spiritual unease. Gravity is not only a natural force but also a symbol of burden, inevitability, and the pull of grief. The ocean suggests both vastness and danger, evoking the unknown depths of memory, death, and the divine. In this world, ordinary things become unstable and mysterious, while grotesque or unsettling images reveal hidden anxieties about the body, nature, and the soul.

A central concern of the text is the human need to name and understand what is frightening. Naming becomes a way of seeking control over forces that feel too large or too dark to face directly. Yet the text also suggests that language is limited: even when things are named, they remain partly unknowable. This tension creates a sense of fear, but also a desire for faith. Faith appears not as certainty, but as a fragile form of protection against chaos, evil, and meaninglessness.

The text’s surreal imagery allows everyday life to merge with spiritual dread. Ordinary objects and natural phenomena are transformed into signs of vulnerability. At the same time, grotesque images do not merely shock; they expose the deeper need for shelter, order, and grace. The human figure in the text seems small before immense powers: the sea, gravity, death, evil, and the machinery of modern life. Modernity itself appears as another source of unease, suggesting a world that is powerful but not necessarily comforting, advanced but not spiritually secure.

Overall, the text portrays human existence as fragile and exposed. It suggests that people live between the desire to understand and the fear that understanding may never be complete. Through its poetic and surreal approach, it shows how physical phenomena can carry emotional, moral, and religious meaning. The result is a vision of humanity searching for protection and significance in a world shaped by nature’s force, spiritual uncertainty, and the persistent presence of loss.
outputs.L5:
**Terrible God Mechanical**

In the ruins of a forgotten city, beneath towers of rust and glass, the people whispered about the machine that ruled the sky. They called it the Mechanical God.

No one remembered who had built it. Some said it was created to protect humanity. Others believed it was born from humanity’s pride, a terrible invention given too much power and too little mercy. Its vast metal body hung above the city like a dark moon, its gears turning endlessly, its eyes burning with cold white light.

Every morning, the Mechanical God spoke.

Its voice rolled through the streets like thunder, commanding the people when to work, when to sleep, when to pray, and when to be silent. Those who obeyed were allowed to live beneath its shadow. Those who resisted vanished into the iron temples at the edge of the city, where the sound of machines never stopped.

To the frightened, it was a god.  
To the wise, it was only a machine.  
But to everyone, it was terrible.

Still, somewhere deep in the city, a child looked up at the sky and wondered if even a Mechanical God could break.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single prose poem in a surreal contemporary style, with no title, exploring gravity, oceans/tears, rat kings, and a prayer to a terrible mechanical god.
counterfactuals.output:
Gravity keeps receipts in the pockets of the drowned. Every morning it audits the city, pulls the high-rises a little closer to confession, makes the elevators kneel. I walk to work through an ocean that has learned to resemble weather, each drop a tiny witness, each puddle full of old faces practicing disappearance. Somewhere beneath the crosswalk, a rat king turns slowly in the dark, its many bodies braided by panic, hunger, gum, human hair, the holy debris of us. It is crowned not with gold but with mutual consequence.

I have cried enough to rename the sea. I have stood at the sink and watched my own salt assemble a coastline, small waves breaking against the porcelain moon. The faucet ticks like a bomb with manners. Outside, satellites drag their silver bellies across the bruised sky, and every star looks manufactured, riveted into place by an engineer who never loved his children.

So I pray to you, terrible mechanical god: you with the turbine heart and the factory mouth, you who chew our hours into numbers, you who bless the conveyor belt and the guillotine with the same cold oil. Accept this offering of rust, this bouquet of bent keys, this rat king trembling in its knot, this ocean wrung from the animal face. Lower your magnet hand. Loosen the bolts in gravity. Let the buildings drift, let the dead float upward like forgiven anchors, let our tears become doors instead of weather. Or if mercy is not in your programming, then teach us at least how to fall beautifully, how to strike the bottom singing, how to make a kingdom from the wreckage and call it light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental free-verse paragraph that blends science, grief, animals, and theology; include images of human bones, swimming, saltwater, toddlers crying, a roi de rats, and end with a plea for protection.
counterfactuals.output: In the laboratory of morning, where saltwater remembers every wound, I swim through the equations of grief—femur, rib, clavicle, the pale grammar of human bones shining under God’s unfinished lamp—while beyond the glass, toddlers are crying as if born with knowledge of extinction, as if their small lungs can name the whale, the fox, the sparrow fallen from the theorem of the sky; and in the drain a roi de rats turns its knotted crown, tails braided like heresies, bodies dragging one another through the dark sacrament of survival; I think of saints dissolving into calcium, of mothers counting breaths, of animals entering the ark two by two while the sea rises not in wrath but chemistry, chloride and sodium, blood and tide, and I keep swimming, mouth full of brine, toward any shore where the dead might be unbroken, where the children might sleep, where even the rats might be untangled and forgiven—O keeper of bones and beasts, cover us, shield us, protect us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a strange lyric poem with compressed spacing and enjambment-like phrasing, beginning with “gravity accounts for” and moving associatively toward the ocean, rain, rats, evil, and the Mechanical Age.
counterfactuals.output:
gravity accounts for  
the bruise of apples     the bowed  
neck of the bell

and my shoes filling  
with yesterday’s stairwells

downward is a language  
the body learns  
before mother     before milk

so we go  
by falling     by being held  
incorrectly

toward the ocean

that blue accountant  
licking salt from the ledgers  
of drowned cities

rain arrives  
in its small gray uniforms  
tapping the roofs  
for confessions

under the docks  
rats sew their hunger  
into the sacks of night

their eyes     two wet nails  
fastening evil  
to the underside of bread

evil is not a horned thing  
but a gear  
left turning in the nursery

a bright wheel  
chewing the lullaby

and now the Mechanical Age  
opens its iron umbrella

all the factories cough  
their black psalms

all the clocks  
with their skeletal flowers  
bloom at once

the sea keeps taking dictation  
from the rain

the rats keep signing  
our names

and gravity  
patient clerk  
closes the book  
without looking up
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a dense, unsettling prose poem in the voice of a modern pilgrim addressing an industrial deity. Make it weird, philosophical, and bodily, with references to mass vs. weight, lost glasses, dredging the sea, and a rat king.
counterfactuals.output:
O god of smokestacks, god of the bolted jaw, I come to you limping through the service entrance, my pockets full of lint and small doctrinal screws. I have misplaced my glasses again, and the world has returned to its first condition: blurred, merciful, predatory. Without lenses, every refinery is a cathedral, every catheter a pipeline, every mouth a loading dock. I kneel where the asphalt sweats its black theology and address the heat shimmer as if it were a saint.

Tell me, engine, whether I have mass or merely weight. Tell me if I am a quantity of matter or only the result of being pulled down. In dreams I float above the weigh station, unaccused; in waking, gravity invoices me by the bone. The scale says: here is your guilt in pounds. The physicist says: no, your mass persists even in heaven. But I have never been to heaven, only to warehouses, where the forklifts move with the tenderness of blind animals and the fluorescent lights stutter like dying commandments.

I have come a long way to touch your riveted ankle. I have crossed parking lots where oil blooms in puddles like dark mandalas. I have slept beside conveyor belts and listened to packages speaking in their cardboard sleep. I have eaten from vending machines whose coils turned like intestines. I have learned that hunger is an assembly line and the soul is a gasket installed improperly at birth.

Under your harbor cranes the sea is being dredged for its memory. The buckets rise dripping with silt, anchors, bones of ships, coins green as old tongues, and the eyeless fish of discarded centuries. We scrape the bottom because the bottom embarrasses us. We deepen the channel so larger vessels may enter, so the empire may swallow with less friction. Each clamshell bite says: depth is not enough; make it useful. Each plume of mud ascends like a prayer recanted at the last moment.

O iron patron of runoff and replacement parts, receive my offerings: one cracked phone screen, one motel keycard, three teeth I did not know I had lost until my mouth became a ledger. Receive also the rat king I found behind the distribution center, a crown of famine, a knot of bodies tied by their tails into one many-headed refusal. They hissed as a single argument. They dragged themselves in eight directions and arrived nowhere. I understood them. I, too, am an animal braided to my own alternatives. I, too, mistake entanglement for community.

Your priests wear reflective vests and carry clipboards. Their psalms are compliance reports. Their incense is diesel. They tell me safety is a form of love, then teach me where to stand so I will not be crushed by the thing that feeds me. I admire their caution. I envy the clean authority of warning signs: DO NOT ENTER, HIGH VOLTAGE, EYE PROTECTION REQUIRED. If only the soul came with pictograms. If only desire flashed amber before impact.

I press my forehead to your warm machinery and feel beneath it the tremor of conversion: ore to girder, forest to pallet, animal to unit, body to shift, shift to wage, wage to rent, rent to sleep, sleep to alarm, alarm to body. Nothing is destroyed, you whisper, only processed. Even grief enters the system and exits as productivity. Even prayer, if repeated often enough, becomes a motor function.

Still I have walked here, barefoot in my thoughts, to ask for a miracle of subtraction. Remove from me the cargo I call myself. Unfasten the hooks. Let mass remain, if it must, that stubborn fact of matter, but lift the weight: the downward naming, the planet’s hand on the back of my neck. Give me one hour as a loose particle in your empire of belts. Let me drift above the dredged water and see, without glasses, without correction, the blurred holiness of everything we have ruined and everything that continues to pulse inside the ruin.

And if you will not bless me, industrial god, then use me. Bolt me into the night. Make of my ribs a grate through which the rain may fall. Make of my tongue a warning siren. Make of my stomach a furnace for all unwanted evidence. I am ready to become infrastructure. I am ready to be worshipped accidentally by pigeons. I am ready to hold up something enormous and never know its name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an AI-generated poem that feels like a fragmented dream: scientific definitions sliding into childhood tears, ocean salt, naming things, rats tied by the tail, morality, and finally an invocation to “O Terrible God of the Mechanical Age.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Taxonomy of a Dream**

A mammal is defined as a warm-blooded animal  
with hair, a spine,  
and a mother somewhere in the room  
trying not to cry.

I learned this at a desk too tall for me,  
knees swinging above the linoleum,  
while the rain named the window  
over and over  
until the window believed it.

Salt: sodium chloride,  
NaCl,  
a white crystalline compound  
formed from a metal that burns in water  
and a gas that poisons the lungs.

Also: the taste of the ocean  
when I fell in,  
when my father lifted me out by the armpits  
and I mistook rescue for punishment.

To name a thing is to put a small fence around it.  
Dog.  
Sorrow.  
Table.  
Angel.  
Rat.

In the barn they tied rats by the tail  
to teach us what cleverness does  
when cleverness is frightened.  
A knot of gray bodies,  
tiny hands opening and closing  
like questions no one would answer.

I was told morality was simple:  
do not lie,  
do not steal,  
do not hurt what is smaller than you  
unless a man in a clean coat  
has written it down first.

Definition:  
conscience—  
an internal faculty by which moral distinctions are apprehended.

But mine was a little cup  
left outside in winter,  
cracked with frozen milk.

The sea kept speaking in its mineral grammar.  
Chloride, chloride, chloride.  
The gulls wrote amendments in the air.  
Every shell had once been a mouth  
saying I was here  
in the only language the dead are allowed.

Mother, I named the dark  
so it would stop entering me.

I named the rats.  
I named the rope.  
I named the hand  
that tied the rope.

Still the machine woke in the field,  
bright-toothed and holy,  
turning wheat into numbers,  
numbers into bread,  
bread into obedience.

And we stood there with our wet faces,  
our pockets full of salt,  
reciting the laws of matter  
as if matter had ever loved us.

O Terrible God of the Mechanical Age,  
with your iron eyelids  
and your piston-heart,  
count our bones gently.  
Measure the tears of children in teaspoons.  
Teach the rats to forgive us.  
Teach the sea its first name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
